dataset.name: SPRUCE S1 Bog Porewater, Groundwater, and Stream Chemistry Data: 2011-2013
description: This data set reports the chemistry of S1 bog porewater, outlet stream water, and groundwater from upland wells from 2011 through 2013. The experimental work is to be conducted in a Picea mariana [black spruce] - Sphagnum spp. bog forest in northern Minnesota, 40 km north of Grand Rapids, in the USDA Forest Service Marcell Experimental Forest (MEF).

These data provide information for studies of the biogeochemical status of the bog and surrounding groundwater aquifer. Porewater samples were collected from one nest of 6 piezometers installed in a hollow in the south end of the S1 bog to characterize solute chemistry depth profiles. Peat porewater was collected from piezometers that opened at 0, 0.3, 0.5, 1, 2, and 3 m depths below hollow surfaces. Samples were collected weekly (2011) or monthly (2012 & 2013) when the samplers were not frozen (typically June - November). Stream water was sampled weekly (2011-2013) from the outlet of the S1 bog (located on the southern edge of the bog). Four groundwater wells located in the uplands of the S1 watershed were sampled monthly in 2013. Bog water level data are also reported for the S1 bog. Water samples were analyzed for pH, specific conductivity, nutrient concentrations (ammonium, nitrate, soluble reactive phosphorus, total nitrogen, total phosphorus), cation concentrations (calcium, potassium, magnesium, sodium, aluminum, iron, manganese, silicon, strontium), anion concentrations (chloride, sulfate), and total organic carbon concentrations.
Please refer to the provided documentation (SPRUCE_S1_bog_porewater_groundwater_and_stream_chemistry_data_2011_2013_*.pdf) for maps, photos, and measurement details.

measurementTechnique:
Field Sampling and Measurements:
Porewater chemistry sampling:
Peat porewater was collected from a nest of 6 piezometers that were installed in a hollow in the south end of the S1 bog (Figures 1, 2). Each piezometer was 5.1 cm in diameter and had a 10-cm long screened section (machined 0.25-mm slots) to collect porewater at 0 m, 0.3 m, 0.5 m, 1.0 m, 2.0 m, and 3.0 m depths into the peat. The threaded piezometer joints were sealed with PTFE tape. The piezometers were installed so the top of the 10-cm screened section was at the reported depth (i.e., the 1.0 m piezometer collected water from 1.0 to 1.1 m depth). The top of the screened section of the 0 m piezometer was at the hollow surface. Piezometers were installed in spring and summer 2011 and purged multiple times until the water was free of particles. Porewater sampling for chemical analyses began in July 2011. Water samples were collected approximately weekly in 2011, and monthly in 2012 and 2013 whenever water in the piezometers was not frozen, typically June to November. There were 2 sampling dates in April 2012 when water in the 0, 2.0, and 3.0 m piezometers was not frozen and could be sampled, but the remaining depths were not sampled. The 0, 0.5, and 1.0 m piezometers on occasion did not yield enough water for chemical analysis. The piezometers were purged the day before (for the slower-filling 2.0 and 3.0 m piezometers) or several hours before (0 to 1.0 m piezometers) each sampling event so that water samples were fresh. An unfiltered water sample was pumped from each piezometer using a peristaltic pump connected to a 0.64-cm diameter PVC sampling tube that was located inside each piezometer (Figure 3). The water was pumped into a clean 250-mL HDPE bottle that was rinsed 3 times with collected water before being filled. Samples were not filtered as the collected water had few particulates. All samples were immediately placed on ice and then refrigerated until laboratory analysis.

Streamwater Chemistry Sampling:
The S1 outlet stream (Figures 1, 4) was sampled weekly in 2011 (biweekly until July and then weekly), 2012, and 2013 for chemistry. Samples were collected from ~March/April to November/December each year. An unfiltered water sample was collected using a dipper into a clean 250-mL HDPE bottle that was rinsed 3 times with the collected water before being filled. Samples were not filtered as the collected water had few particulates. All samples were immediately placed on ice and then refrigerated until laboratory analysis.

Groundwater Chemistry Sampling:
Groundwater was sampled from 4 fully screened wells (3.3 to 8.2 m deep, 0.03-m diameter galvanized steel pipe) in the uplands of the S1 watershed weekly from August to November 2013 (Figure 1). A bailer was used to collect water from the well, and an unfiltered sample was placed into a clean 250-mL HDPE bottle that was rinsed 3 times with the collected water before being filled. Samples were not filtered as the collected water had few particulates. All samples were immediately placed on ice and then refrigerated until laboratory analysis.

Bog Water Level:
Water height in the EM1 well was measured every 30 minutes using a TruTrack WT-VO Water Height Probe. The 1.723 m stainless steel well casing is fully screened, with about 0.2 m above the hollow surface. The WT-VO sensor was re-calibrated each year and the depth relative to an adjacent hollow was remeasured with each calibration. Values were recorded as a depth of water relative to an adjacent hollow surface. A negative value represented water below the surface and a positive value represented water above the surface. The data were first QA:QC’ed by removing erratic fluctuations in water depths or periods when the well was known to be frozen.
The well elevation did not move since it was anchored into deep peat. Because peat elevation fluctuates, the datum for reporting water depth relative to hollow surface was subject to fluctuations over time as vegetation grew during the summer, organic matter accumulated or decomposed, buoyant organic matter rose or fell, snowpacks compacted organic matter, and concrete frost heaved organic matter. We compared the EM1 water level data to water level elevation data from a well near the middle of the S1 bog to eliminate shifting datums from season to season or year to year for water levels and to gap fill during frozen periods (Figure 1).
The S1 bog well has been operated by the USDA Forest Service since September 1960 (Sebestyen et al. 2011). The datum is on a deeply anchored structure and water levels have been reported as elevation above mean sea level. Water level was recorded using a float-driven stripchart recorder, which was housed inside a heated enclosure. The maximum daily water level was read and recorded in a spreadsheet.
Water table elevation at the S1 bog well was converted to a water table depth by subtracting 412.11 m from the water table elevation (412.11 m was the elevation on days during 2011 when water level depth at EM1 was 0).
The daily high water depth in the EM1 was then determined for comparisons to the S1 bog well record. To reduce bias from days with incomplete recording of values, data were only used for days with at least 48 of 96 values recorded in a two day running period. Step shifts in water depths at EM1 occurred at times of calibrations, frost heaving, or other physical jostling of the WT-VO sensor. Step shifts were identified through visual inspection of graphs of water depth over time relative to the S1 bog well and bivariate plots of water depths at EM1 and the S1 bog well. Step shifts were removed by adding or subtracting an offset to the water depth for the duration of a step shift, which resulted in data aligning along a 1:1 relationship in bivariate plots. The slope and intercept of the relationship between the corrected EM1 water depths and S1 bog well were calculated and used in a linear relationship to predict the EM1 water depths over the entire period and fill gaps during periods when the EM1 well data were missing or the well was frozen.

Analytical Methods:
Water samples were analyzed for pH, specific conductivity, and cation concentrations, anion concentrations, nutrient concentrations (nitrate, ammonium, soluble reactive phosphorus, total nitrogen, total phosphorus), and total organic carbon concentrations at the USFS’s analytical lab in Grand Rapids, MN.
